newsitem.title: ISRAEL: ISRAEL TREASURY PRESENTS PLAN FOR ECONOMIC REFORM.
newsitem.headline: ISRAEL TREASURY PRESENTS PLAN FOR ECONOMIC REFORM.

text.p: Israel's Treasury presented to government ministers on Thursday a wide sweeping programme of structural reforms aimed at reviving economic growth in 1998.
The programme, which will be discussed by the cabinet on Sunday, include plans for privatisation, capital market reform, an end to various monopolies, and further foreign currency liberalisation.
A copy of the proposal was made available to the press on Thursday.
The Treasury proposed increasing investment in infrastructure by 20 percent in 1998 to 13.1 billion shekels.
The increased investment would be aimed at, among others, public transport and roads; railroad projects, sewage and water projects and natural gas projects.
The document said it seeks to make public transport and roads more efficient and a complete redrafting of all public transport routes particularly in metropolitan areas before the end of June 1998.
A natural gas tender for a natural gas operator is aimed to be issued by February 1, 1998, the document said.

The document envisages an increase in competition in the economy, including competition in bus routes and the fuel market, ending Israel Electric Corp's transmission monopoly for large consumers, changing the law to give more strength to the anti-trust authority, opening the cement market to competition, opening flights to the north of Israel to competition.

The Treasury has proposed a capital market reform which in effect is a reduced version of a reform shelved by the cabinet because of a controversial tax on short term savings. The revised capital market reform omits this tax.

While the document gives no details, the Treasury has set a minimum 1998 privatisation target of four billion shekels, including the sale of the government's controlling shares in banks. The receipts will be used to fund debt, the document said.
The government set a four billion shekel privatisation target in 1997 but hopes with the sale of a controlling stake in Bank Hapoalim it will raise a total of seven billion shekels this year.

The document recommends further liberalisation in the forex market. No details were given, but the document recommended that the Bank of Israel proceed toward a fully convertible currency by mid 1998.
The document envisages tightening controls on unemployment payments and fixing a 7,500 shekel fine on every foreign worker employed without licence.
